cards.title: Soil is not just dirt
cards.body: Good soil is roughly 45% minerals, 25% water, 25% air, and 5% organic matter. Roots need all four: minerals feed the plant, water carries nutrients, air lets roots breathe, and organic matter (compost) holds it all together.

cards.title: Know your soil type
cards.body: Squeeze a handful of damp soil: sandy soil crumbles instantly and drains fast, clay forms a tight ball and holds water, loam holds a loose shape and crumbles when poked — that's the jackpot. Most vegetables want loam.
The finger test beats any gadget: push your finger 2 inches into the soil. Dry? Water. Moist? Wait. Soggy? Your plant is drowning — improve drainage before it rots.
Starting tomatoes: sow seeds ¼ inch deep in seed mix (not garden soil), keep at 70-75°F, and they'll sprout in 5-10 days. A seed planted twice as deep as it is wide is the rule of thumb.

cards.q: Your damp soil forms a tight sticky ball. What type is it?
cards.explain: Clay particles are tiny and pack tightly, holding water and forming balls. Sandy soil crumbles; loam holds a loose shape.

flashcards.front: What are the four parts of healthy soil?
Which soil type do most vegetables prefer?
flashcards.back: Loam — holds shape loosely, drains well, rich in nutrients.

flashcards.front: How deep should you plant a seed?
flashcards.back: About twice as deep as the seed is wide.

flashcards.front: What does the finger test tell you?
flashcards.back: Whether soil 2 inches down is dry (water), moist (wait), or soggy (drainage problem).

questions.q: Why do roots need air in the soil?
choices: Roots breathe and can suffocate in waterlogged soil
questions.explain: Roots respire like the rest of the plant. Waterlogged soil squeezes out air pockets and roots rot.

questions.q: What does compost (organic matter) do for soil?
choices: Holds nutrients and moisture, feeds soil life
questions.explain: Compost is the glue: it holds water and nutrients, feeds microbes, and improves both sandy and clay soils.

questions.q: You plant bean seeds 3 inches deep and few sprout. What went wrong?
choices: Planted too deep — seedlings ran out of energy
questions.explain: Seeds carry limited stored energy. Buried too deep, the sprout exhausts itself before reaching light.

questions.q: Sandy soil drains in minutes and plants wilt fast. What's the fix?
choices: Mix in compost to hold moisture
questions.explain: Compost acts like a sponge in sandy soil, holding water where roots can reach it.

questions.q: A seed packet says 'sow after last frost.' Why does timing matter?
choices: Cold soil slows germination and frost kills seedlings
Seeds only sprout in summer heat
questions.explain: Most seeds need warm soil to germinate, and tender seedlings die in frost. Timing matches the seed's biology.

cards.title: Water deeply, not daily
cards.body: Shallow daily sprinkles train roots to stay near the surface, where they dry out fast. One deep watering per week pushes roots downward into cool, moist soil — building drought-proof plants. Most vegetables want about 1 inch of water per week.

cards.title: Read the plant, not the calendar
cards.body: Wilting in the morning means thirsty; wilting only in afternoon heat is normal. Yellow lower leaves often mean overwatering, while crispy brown edges mean underwatering. The plant is always telling you something — learn its language.
Water the soil, not the leaves. Wet foliage invites fungal disease; a soaker hose or watering can at the base keeps leaves dry and delivers water where roots actually are.

Tomatoes in July: water deeply 2-3 times per week (about 1-1.5 inches total), mulch 3 inches around the base, and water in the morning so leaves dry by evening. Blossom-end rot? That's inconsistent watering, not a disease.

cards.q: Your plant's lower leaves are yellow and the soil is soggy. What's wrong?
cards.explain: Yellow lower leaves plus soggy soil is classic overwatering — roots are suffocating. Let it dry out.

flashcards.front: How much water do most vegetables need weekly?
flashcards.back: About 1 inch, delivered in deep waterings rather than daily sprinkles.

flashcards.front: Why water deeply instead of daily?
flashcards.back: Deep watering drives roots downward into reliably moist soil; shallow watering keeps roots weak near the surface.
At least 6 hours of direct sunlight per day.
Leaves dry by evening, which prevents fungal disease; less water evaporates than at midday.

questions.q: Two gardeners: one sprinkles 10 minutes daily, one soaks deeply twice a week. Whose plants survive a heatwave?
questions.explain: Deep roots reach cool, moist soil. Shallow roots sit in the layer that dries first.

questions.q: What does 'partial shade' mean for a plant label?
questions.explain: Partial shade plants want some direct sun but shelter from harsh afternoon rays.

questions.q: Your lettuce bolts (flowers) in July heat. What happened?
choices: Heat triggered it to finish its life cycle early
questions.explain: Lettuce is a cool-season crop; heat signals it to bolt and turn bitter. Plant it for spring or fall.

choices: Holds moisture, cools soil, blocks weeds
questions.explain: A 2-3 inch mulch layer is a blanket: it slows evaporation, steadies soil temperature, and smothers weeds.

questions.q: Seedlings stretch tall and floppy on a windowsill. What's missing?
questions.explain: Leggy seedlings are reaching for more light. Move them closer to the window or add a grow light.

cards.title: Know your enemy
cards.body: The usual suspects: aphids (tiny sap-suckers clustering on new growth), slugs (night slime trails and chewed holes), cabbage worms (green caterpillars on brassicas), and spider mites (fine webbing, stippled leaves). Identify before you act — the fix depends on the pest.

cards.title: Start with the gentlest fix
cards.body: Integrated pest management means escalating slowly: handpick first, then blast aphids off with a hose, then insecticidal soap or neem oil, and only then stronger measures. Most infestations never need chemicals — they need attention.
Invite the predators: ladybugs devour aphids, lacewings eat mites, and birds patrol for caterpillars. A garden with flowers for beneficial insects has its own security team working for free.
Aphids on your roses: blast them off with a strong jet of water, repeat every 2-3 days. Still there? Spray insecticidal soap in the evening (never in hot sun). Gone in a week, pollinators unharmed.

cards.q: You find clusters of tiny green insects on new rose shoots. What are they, and what's the first move?
cards.explain: Classic aphids. A water jet knocks most off; escalate only if they return.

flashcards.back: Tiny sap-sucking insects that cluster on new growth and buds.
A plant-derived oil that disrupts insect feeding and reproduction — organic-approved.
Ladybug (eats aphids), lacewing (eats mites), or parasitic wasp.
Growing plants together so one repels pests or helps the other — e.g. marigolds near tomatoes.

questions.q: Why handpick pests before reaching for sprays?
choices: Handpicking is faster for large gardens
It's targeted, free, and harms nothing else
questions.explain: Handpicking removes only the pest. Sprays can kill beneficial insects and pollinators too.

questions.q: Slugs shred your lettuce every night. What's an organic fix?
questions.explain: Slugs drown in sunken beer traps and won't cross copper. Night watering just invites more slugs.

questions.q: Marigolds planted around tomatoes reduce which problem?
questions.explain: Marigold roots release compounds that suppress nematodes, and their scent confuses some pests.

questions.q: You spray insecticide at noon in full sun. What goes wrong?
choices: Leaves burn and pollinators get hit
questions.explain: Sprays + hot sun = leaf burn. Midday is also peak pollinator activity. Spray in the evening.

questions.q: After wiping out every insect with broad spray, aphids return worse than before. Why?
questions.explain: Broad sprays kill ladybugs and lacewings too. Without predators, the fastest breeders — aphids — explode.
